text:
Recent work supports learning substitute/complement relationships when additional supervision exists. [SCRM (2023/2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.14957) constructs separate relationship graphs from click and purchase sequences, then applies denoising and relationship constraints; its experiments report component ablations. Those behavior distinctions are unavailable here. [KGSCL (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089360802500070X) uses Amazon metadata’s explicit substitute/complement relationships to guide substitution and insertion augmentations. Those relationship fields also exceed the supplied data contract. Neither establishes that titles/descriptions plus a single interaction stream reliably identify complements.

Text-based sequential recommendation results require care: [Recformer (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13731) combines language/recommendation pretraining; its reported no-pretraining ablation performs substantially worse. [WhitenRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10602) explicitly depends on pretrained text embeddings. These results therefore do not establish gains under the train-from-scratch restriction. A feasible experimental hypothesis is a small randomly initialized token-pooling encoder over supplied titles/descriptions, fused with SASRec ID embeddings and trained using observed next-item supervision. Compare ID-only, text-only, fused, and shuffled-text controls using the fixed macro validation HR@10; separately inspect sparse-item behavior. Treat learned directional transitions as predictive associations, not verified complement labels. Text overlap can share statistical strength, but these sources provide no basis for inferring ownership, compatibility, or an unmet need from similarity alone.
